questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I really wanted to experience the amazing nature that British Columbia has to offer. The beautiful mountain views, the giant trees, and mirror lakes among others. 
I was also intrigued by the relatively new conversation about reconciliation regarding the colonial powers and their history with the original peoples of the land. UBC is placed on the traditional, ancestral, and unceded territory of the Mosqueam People, which is both important and interesting to acknowledge and learn about. This played a central role in my choosing since I wanted to do my electives in Anthropology. UBC is known for having a great Anthropology programme.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was relatively easy. Imagine Day gave a great introduction and Go Global was helpful and accessible.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: When I arrived I was still waiting for a positive response from a professor regarding enrolment into his course, since it was already full. I was lucky to enrol during my first day, since someone dropped the course, however it turned out to be an online course, which they rarely allow exchange student into. Go Global were, however, very helpful and let me take the course.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: The reason since I rate it 4 instead of 5 is that there was quite the line and I had to wait for a while to get help.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
It was pretty stressful and difficult. Before arriving I responded to a lot of posts about housing and contacted many people online, but there was many scammers as well as a lot of people applying. Upon arrival I lived in an AirBnB and spend the first 3-4 days looking for housing from morning till dawn. I signed up for a lot of paid websites and texted everyone I could find on local Facebook groups and on Craigslist. I also called several Real Estate companies, without any luck. I ended up finding my apartment online on Craigslist. 
One mayor recommendation is not to pay anything to anyone before having seen the apartment in real live. I tried more than once, that people would go to great lengths to trick me into paying for a scam. 
An as an extension I would recommend waiting until you're there to commit to housing.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
I was lucky that my boyfriend was also going on exchange to UBC and we found ourselves a private apartment together off-campus. That was really nice and we both enjoyed living there. 
However, if you're going by yourself I would recommend trying to find a room with other people - either some from your own home university or other student already living in Vancouver. There are plenty of possibilities for finding rooms online if you're looking for a single room. 
Personally, I was very happy living off campus because the city was much more accessible and I got out and experienced much more than my friends living on campus.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There was very limited options for couples wanting to live together on campus. We were supposed to get an offer from an on-campus housing, that we had applied to, but they messed up and we accidentally got deleted from the list of applicants and had to start over.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: As mentioned before, I had some trouble registering into one course, that I had to take for my exchange to be approved, which caused me some stress. I tried calling and e-mailing the professor multiple times without response. I also contacted the Go Global counsellors, but they couldn't help me. At last I was lucky to register online, when someone suddenly dropped the course.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I didn't quite follow the official registration process, because I wanted to make sure, that I got the courses I wanted. Also, when at first, I did follow the registration process which included making a priority list of 10 courses, but I only got one of them - only one out of the three I had gotten pre-approved. Also, one of the courses I needed was a graduate course, but I could apply or register for grad courses online, but had to wait until end August to apply. Instead I contacted the professor directly and he helped me register.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I didn't really find a lot of help available during the Summer Vacation. But I just decided to contact different people via e-mail, e.g. professors and student administrations.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: As I have already explained, I ended up registering for all the courses I wanted. So very successful.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: 12.	Be proactive and reach out to professors, student administrations and Go Global if you don't get the courses you want. Also, even if you don't get the course at first, show up to class and let the professor know that you're interested in registering. Also, in case a spot becomes available you won't have missed classes already.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
I had two 400 point courses - one called PSYC413 in Social and Personality Development, which was online and didn't seem that difficult, but I enjoyed the learning method, that consisted in reading a few research articles and then answer questions on their subjects, research results etc. 
My other course ANTH400 History of Anthropology was definitely the best course of them all. It was pretty advanced in regards to the theories tought, but it was incredibly giving and I learned so much about the dark history of the Anthropological discipline and especially the history of Canada. 
I also had a 500 point course in Qualitative Methods in Anthropology. This course was difficult because it was pretty poorly structured and there wasn't a lot of guidance, since most participants were PHD-students doing their own research separately and having their own counsellor outside of the course.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: At UBC there are no formal rules or restrictions on how to teach or structure a course. Therefore it is difficult comparing it to UCPH. But generally at UBC your final grade is made up of different components such as attendance, participation, smaller assignments, and class presentations, and a final assignment instead of only having a final exam.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
PSYC413 Social and Personality Development
ANTH400 History of Anthropology
ANTH516 Qualitative Research Methods of Anthropology

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would really recommend History of Anthropology to anyone interested in learning about anthropology. I have already learned a little about the main theories introduced but here I really learned it in context. My professor Sara Shneiderman was very inspirational and a great teacher. She initially said that this course was advanced for anthropology majors but she allowed me to stay and I ended up getting an A.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: It was surprisingly expensive to buy fresh groceries. Compared to Denmark it cost quite a bit more. Also, the housing prices are pretty high in Vancouver, but this is a problem for almost everyone living there. There is a big housing problem resulting in a lot of homelessness.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: As said, groceries were more expensive which surprised me because we're always told that Denmark is so expensive. However, going out eating or getting drinks was less expensive compared to Copenhagen. And also books were free for my courses.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There was a lot of options, but of course less when you're only there for one semester. I joined the surf-club and the film society. A lot of my friends were also part of the outdoor club, but I didn't find it necessary. I often went to the Gallery with my friends for karaoke nights, which was a really fun event and a good way to hang out.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Definitely the surf club! We went to Tofino to surf and it was so fun and a great way to meet new friends - also Canadians!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend driving to Banff! It's so beautiful and even though it's a 10 hour drive it was so worth it! Also, of course, go for hikes in Garibaldi and ski in Whistler. 
I also went to North Cascades in Washington state for a weekend and hiked around Mt. Baker. I spend my midterm break in Maui, Hawaii, which was so amazing.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. The city's culture is pretty similar to Copenhagen. But the city wasn't that interesting in terms of culture and social events. I loved having the nature so close by.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: At first I thought that they were very unsociable, but then I realised that because of their school system, they don't necessarily know a lot of other students and are actually pretty happy to engage with other students. So talk to then, go to social events and be open to them. I met some local students and they were friendly and fun, but also pretty young and immature compared to the other exchange students that became my close friends.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not a lot really. Mostly that other students were younger than me.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Their relationship and appreciation of nature. They are so aware of the nature around them and the fact, that nature is 'bear territory' etc. I just really appreciate how they spend a lot of time in and with nature and have a lot of respect for the animals.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Be prepared for the different ways of teaching and learning as it requires more active participation and attendance. But also reflect on your goals for the exchange - do you want to learn a lot and get good grades or do you just want to do the minimal to pass? 
2. Try to create a schedule where you only go to class twice a week. This is very possible as many courses are either on Mondays and Wednesday or on Tuesday and Thursdays. This way you have a lot of time to go on adventure. 
3. This is the most important one for me, but go on adventure! Really prioritise going on trips, hiking, surfing, skiing. British Columbia has some of the most beautiful nature you'll ever find, so really try to go and experience the most. Especially while the weather is still nice. In my experience going on hikes together is really a great way to make friends and get to know one another.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you find housing on campus really prioritise to go out and experience the city. There's a lot of cute and cool areas around the city. Especially in Mount Pleasant.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: If I should chose only one part, I would probably say that I realised how much I love being active in nature. But also realising that I don't have to go all the way around the world to experience this kind of nature. I have really come to appreciate living in Europe, having so much culture and history and amazing nature around me.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Definitely the social aspect. The other people from University of Copenhagen were pretty aggressive at first wanting to make friends and that resulted in a lot of social drama and people feeling excluded. Because of this I was pretty shocked and didn't really want to be part of a friend group that acted badly towards others. Instead I met other exchange students from other parts of Europa, whom I became super close with.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
